# Seawall Admin Console User Manual

> Seawall is a network protection device. The Admin Console is its web interface: watch traffic and blocked events, manage access lists (ACLs) and the interfaces that apply them, and save the configuration. This file is for AI assistants helping a user of the console: when they ask how to use a feature, answer from this manual and use the exact names shown in the interface (menus, buttons, fields).

## For AI assistants

- Describe only what this manual covers. The DDoS Protection, HTTP Flood, CC Protection, Brute-Force Protection and Logs pages currently show "Coming soon" and can't be used yet; don't invent settings for them.
- Access list changes (adding or deleting an entry or a list, applying a list to an interface or removing it) take effect as soon as the user clicks the dialog's button or confirms, but they are not saved: a device restart loses them until someone clicks "Save Config" at the top right. Users often miss this, so mention it when it's relevant.
- Applying an extended list (100 to 199) to an interface drops all incoming traffic the list doesn't permit, even when the list is empty, and that can cut off the user's own connection to the console. Before suggesting it, make sure the list permits what must keep working, such as the console itself (TCP port 8443); "Basic protection" in New List does. "Test a packet" on the interface's tab shows what a list would do to a given packet. If the user is already cut off, restarting the device restores the saved configuration, as long as the change wasn't saved with "Save Config".
- If you don't know, say so, and suggest the user ask their device administrator.

## Logging in and out

- Open the console's address (for example `https://<device>:8443/`), enter the "User name" and "Password", and click "Log In".
- A user name is 1 to 32 letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens, and can't start with a dot or a hyphen. A password is at most 256 bytes, with no line breaks.
- Messages you may see:
  - "Wrong user name or password": check what you typed; it is case-sensitive.
  - "Too many login attempts. Try again in a minute.": too many failed logins in a short time. Wait a minute.
  - "The device is not responding. Please try again later.": the device's services are briefly unavailable. If it keeps happening, contact the administrator.
- A login lasts a fixed time and can't be extended. One minute before it ends the console warns "Your session expires in 1 minute. Save what you are editing."; when it ends it says "Your session has expired. Please log in again." and goes to the login page. After logging in again you are back on the page you were on.
- Reloading the page keeps you logged in; closing the browser tab logs you out.
- To log out: click your user name at the top right and choose "Log out".

## Layout

- Menu on the left: Dashboard, Access Lists, DDoS Protection, HTTP Flood, CC Protection, Brute-Force Protection, Logs. The arrow on the menu's edge collapses or expands it.
- Header: the current page's name on the left; on the right the "Unsaved changes" tag, the "Save Config" button (administrators only), the theme button, the "Help" button and the user name menu.
- Theme: the round icon button in the header, left of "Help" (a monitor, sun or moon, for the current choice). Click it and choose System (the default: light or dark as the computer is set), Light or Dark. The choice is kept in this browser only.
- "Help" opens a panel with the help for the current page. "Full manual" at the bottom of the panel shows this whole manual, and "This page" goes back.

## Roles

- Administrator (admin): can use everything, and sees the "Save Config" button.
- User (user): doesn't see "Save Config" or the "Unsaved changes" tag, and the Access Lists page says "Administrators only": only administrators can view or change the access lists.

## Dashboard

Shows the device's live state. It refreshes every 5 seconds (paused while the browser tab is in the background, and refreshed at once when you come back to it).

- Inbound (pps): packets per second coming into the device now.
- Dropped (pps): packets per second the device is blocking and dropping now.
- Active ACL Entries: how many access list entries are in effect: the entries of the lists that interfaces apply.
- SYN Protection: whether SYN flood protection is on ("On" or "Off").
- Traffic: inbound and dropped traffic over time. Hover over the chart to see the values at a moment; click a legend entry to hide or show that line.
- Recent Blocked Events: the latest blocked traffic, at most 10 entries, newest first. Columns: Time, Source IP, Type, Target, Action. Types: ACL deny, SYN Flood, HTTP Flood, CC attack, Brute force. The action is currently always "Drop".

## Access Lists

Access lists (ACLs) allow or block incoming traffic, in the same numbered, Cisco-style form as the device's command line. The page is organised by interface: one tab per interface shows everything that happens to traffic arriving on it, in order. Administrators only.

### How access lists work

- Each list has a number. Lists 1 to 99 are standard: they match only the source address. Lists 100 to 199 are extended: they match the protocol, source and destination addresses, ports, and optionally established connections or replies.
- A list is made of entries. Each entry has a "Seq" (sequence number, 1 to 65535), an action (permit or deny) and what it matches. The device stores it as a line in Cisco syntax, for example `permit tcp any any eq 22`, and may rewrite what was typed in its own form (a network `198.51.100.0/24` is shown back as `198.51.100.0 0.0.0.255`).
- An interface applies lists to its incoming traffic only: at most one standard and one extended list. A list does nothing until an interface applies it. A list can be applied on several interfaces; a change to it applies on all of them.
- A packet arriving on an interface goes through two stages:
  - Stage 1, the standard list (if any): the first entry, in Seq order, whose source matches decides. Deny drops the packet. Permit, or no matching entry, goes on to stage 2. So a standard list is a block list; a permit in it only matters as an exception placed before a deny that covers the same source.
  - Stage 2, the extended list (if any): the first matching entry decides, permit passes and deny drops. A packet no entry matches is dropped (the implicit deny), even when the list is empty. With no extended list, everything that gets past stage 1 passes.
- Outgoing traffic isn't filtered. Non-first IPv4 fragments skip stage 2, and the device may be set to drop IPv4 fragments altogether. Traffic that isn't IPv4 (ARP, IPv6) always passes.
- A list holds at most 64 entries if standard, 128 if extended. If a list applied to an interface has more (for example after changes from the command line), the device refuses the whole configuration and keeps running the previous one, so no access list change takes effect until the list is trimmed. The page shows "k of 64 entries" (or "of 128") on each list, in amber from 90% full, and doesn't let a change go over.
- Access lists are for rules you write by hand: who may reach which service, and sources you want blocked. Attack traffic is meant to be blocked automatically by DDoS Protection (that page is coming soon); don't suggest building a block list of attack sources by hand.

### The page

- A row of tabs: one per interface that has lists, each with a tag: "Filtered" (the engine is filtering it), "Not on this device" (the configuration names an interface the device doesn't have), or "Not filtered". After a divider, "Lists not in use", with how many there are. On the right, "+ Apply lists to another interface".
- The selected tab is part of the page's address (for example `/acl?iface=eth0`), so a reload or a shared link opens the same tab.

### An interface's tab

1. The status line says whether the lists are in force on this interface. It refreshes every 5 seconds (paused while the browser tab is in the background):
   - Enforced (green): the lists shown are in force. Also shows the engine's Passed and Dropped packet counters, for all interfaces together; there are no counters per entry.
   - Applying (blue): the latest change hasn't reached the engine yet; the interface may still run the previous lists. It normally becomes Enforced within seconds.
   - Engine down (red): the engine that enforces the lists isn't running; the device keeps retrying.
   - Refused (red): the engine refused the configuration; the reason is shown below. The interface may still run the previous lists. If the reason is a list with too many entries, a line names the list and how many entries to remove.
   - Off (grey): the device runs without the engine; nothing is filtered.
   - Not on this device: no interface of this name exists, so its lists filter nothing; they start filtering if it appears. Check the name.
   - Not filtered: the engine is running but isn't filtering this interface, or the interface applies no list.
2. "Test a packet" (below).
3. The policy table, with columns Seq, Protocol, Source, Destination, Result, Actions:
   - "Stage 1 · Standard list N", its entries (deny → Drop, permit → Go on to stage 2), then "Anything else → Go on to stage 2". With no standard list it says "No standard list", with an "Add a standard list" button.
   - "Stage 2 · Extended list N", its entries (permit → Pass, deny → Drop), then "Anything else → Drop (implicit)". With none it says "No extended list: everything past stage 1 passes", with an "Add an extended list" button.
   - Each stage heading shows how full the list is ("3 of 64 entries"), and has "Add Entry", "Change list" and "Remove from <interface>". If the list is applied elsewhere too, it says "Also applied on <interfaces>; changes apply there too".
   - Notes under a result: "No effect: nothing after it in this list denies this source" on a standard permit that no later deny overlaps (it changes nothing; a permit placed before an overlapping deny is an exception and does matter, so it has no note). "Never matches: seq N covers it" when an earlier entry already matches everything this one would.
   - Each entry has "Insert below" (Add Entry, positioned right after it) and "Delete". Delete asks in two steps: the first click turns it into a red "Confirm delete" and shows underneath what deleting does, for example that the traffic a permit lets in will fall to the implicit deny; the second click deletes. "Cancel" there leaves it.
   - Below the table: outgoing traffic isn't filtered, non-first fragments skip stage 2 (and the device may drop fragments altogether), and changes take effect at once but only Save Config keeps them.
- If someone else changed the access lists (another administrator, or the command line) since the page showed them, a delete is not made: the page shows the lists as they are now and says so. Check the entry and delete it again.
- An interface left with no list has "Remove <interface> from the configuration" at the bottom.

### Test a packet

Click "Test a packet" above the table to open it; it stays open or closed the next time, in this browser.

- Describe a packet: Protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP, or Other by number), Source address, Destination address, and for TCP and UDP the ports and the kind of packet: New connection (SYN), Established (ACK or RST set; TCP only), or Reply to a connection this device opened.
- "Fill in" buttons prefill fields: This console (TCP to this console's address and port), SSH, HTTPS, DNS, Ping. Every field stays editable.
- The result updates as you type: "Passed" or "Dropped", and the path, for example "Stage 1: no deny matches 203.0.113.9. Stage 2: entry 20 of list 100 (deny tcp any any eq 22) matches." or "... so the implicit deny drops it." The deciding row is highlighted in the table, green for pass and red for drop. Nothing is highlighted while the panel is closed.
- If the lists aren't Enforced yet (Applying, Refused, Engine down), the result adds "(may still be the previous lists)". If the interface isn't filtered at all, it says "Not filtered", then what would happen once enforced.
- A red field isn't a valid address. Until the packet is complete it says "Incomplete — enter ..." and what is missing.
- A blank source port matches only entries without a source port; the result says when that is why an entry didn't match.
- On the device, `reply` entries only match when sw_flowd is tracking the connection; without it they match nothing, whatever the test says. A hint under "Reply to a connection this device opened" says so.
- The console works this out from the lists as shown, the way the device matches packets; the device itself isn't asked.

### Add Entry: stage 1 (a standard list)

The title says where the entry goes, for example "Add to Stage 1 · List 10 (standard · eth0)". Under it: "To block attack traffic automatically, use DDoS Protection.", with a link to that page.

- Action: "Deny (block)" (the default) drops the source; stage 2 never sees it. "Permit (exempt)" lets the source skip the deny entries after it and go on to stage 2: place it before the deny it is an exception to.
- Source: Host (one address, the default), Network (for example `198.51.100.0/24`; the address must have no host bits set, and the error names the right network), Any, or Several: one address or network per line, one entry each. Bad lines are listed with their line numbers; duplicates and addresses already in the list are skipped, and it says how many.
- Position: "At the top", "After seq A, before B" for each gap, or "At the end". By default the entry goes just before the first entry that matches every source (such as `permit any`), since nothing after that is reached; otherwise at the end. Each choice shows the Seq numbers the new entries get. If they don't fit in a gap it says "No room here; choose another position".
- On the right, stage 1 as it will be after the change, new rows highlighted, ending with "anything else goes on to stage 2". Warnings: "Never matches" (an earlier entry already covers the source), "No effect here" (a permit with no later deny it is an exception to), "Drops everything" (deny any), "Large network" (shorter than /16).
- If the list would go over 64 entries, it says "List N can hold at most 64 entries; it has k. Remove some first." and the button is disabled; for Several it also says how many of the lines fit.
- The button says "Add Entry" or "Add N entries". If one of several fails, the ones before it stay added, the rest stay in the box, and the page says which were added.

### Add Entry: stage 2 (an extended list)

A form; the line it builds is shown at the bottom as "Entry", in the device's syntax. Entries are added with the form only; the console has no field for typing the syntax.

- Action: Permit (the default) or Deny.
- Protocol: IP (any protocol), TCP (the default), UDP, ICMP, or Other by number. Other refuses 0 (choose "IP (any protocol)"), and 1, 6 and 17 switch to ICMP, TCP and UDP so the port fields show.
- Source and Destination: Any, Host, or Network (`192.168.1.0/24`).
- Destination port (TCP and UDP): the buttons Any port, SSH 22, DNS 53, HTTP 80, HTTPS 443 and Console (this console's port); or, below them, Equal to another port, a Range (for example 8000 to 8080), Greater than or Less than a port. Add Entry asks for a port until you choose one. Source port: usually Any port; also Equal to, Range, Greater than, Less than, with port numbers 1 to 65535.
- Match (TCP and UDP): All packets; Established connections only (TCP packets with ACK or RST); or Replies to connections this device opened.
- Position: as for stage 1; the default is at the end.
- A list already at 128 entries can't take another: "List N can hold at most 128 entries; it has 128. Remove some first."
- On the right, the list with the new entry in place, ending with the implicit deny. Warnings: "Never matches" (an earlier entry with the same or any protocol, addresses and ports that include the new one's, and no extra condition), "Very broad" (permit any source to any destination on every port: nothing after it is reached), and "The console" (the list doesn't permit this console's TCP port; see below).
- There is no Edit: to change an entry, add the new one and delete the old one.

### Apply lists to an interface

Opened by "+ Apply lists to another interface", "Change list" or "Add a standard/extended list" on a stage heading (interface fixed), and "Apply to an interface" on a list not in use (that list chosen).

- Interface: type the name, for example `eth0`; the configured interfaces are suggested. The console can't list the device's interfaces yet, so it warns when the engine doesn't know the name ("may not exist on this device"). "Same lists as <interface>" chooses both stages as on that interface.
- Stage 1 · Standard list (1-99) and Stage 2 · Extended list (100-199): None, one of the existing lists (with its entry count, its first entry, and "also on <interfaces>"), or New list with a number (the next free one is filled in).
- "Incoming traffic on <interface>, after this" says in a sentence what each stage will do.
- A chosen list over its limit (64 or 128 entries) can't be applied: the page says how many entries to remove first.
- Warnings: "Everything will be dropped" (red) for an empty or new extended list, and the button becomes "Apply anyway"; "The console" (amber) when the extended list doesn't permit this console's TCP port: if you manage the device through this interface, applying it cuts off the console; a note that with no extended list everything stage 1 doesn't deny passes; a note when a list is shared with other interfaces.
- Apply creates new lists, applies the chosen ones (choosing None removes the interface's list for that stage), and opens the interface's tab.
- The change takes effect at once but isn't saved: if it cuts off your access, restarting the device restores the saved configuration.

### Removing a list from an interface

"Remove from <interface>" on a stage heading only stops applying the list there. If no interface uses the list afterwards, the same question asks "List N is no longer used anywhere. Delete it too?": "Keep it" (it moves to Lists not in use) or "Delete list".

### Lists not in use

- "New List" at the top right.
- Two groups: "Not applied to any interface", and "Applied only to interfaces that are not on this device" (they would start filtering if the interface appeared). "None." when a group is empty.
- Each row shows the list's kind and "k of 64 entries" (or "of 128"). Click a row to show its entries, each with a two-step Delete.
- Actions: "Apply to an interface", "Add Entry", "Delete list" (two steps; for the second group it also removes the list from those interfaces), and for the second group "Remove from <interface>".

### New List

- "What is it for?": "Block sources" (a standard list, 1-99: checked first, by source only; for blocklists) or "Allow services" (an extended list, 100-199: lets in what you permit and drops the rest).
- Number: the next free number of that kind is filled in, by tens first. A number out of range or taken is marked red; the numbers in use are listed.
- Start with:
  - Block sources: "Addresses to deny" (one per line, as for Several, at most 64), "Empty", or "A copy of list N".
  - Allow services: "Basic protection (recommended)", "Empty", or "A copy of list N". Basic protection needs the Management network you manage the device from, and creates: permit TCP from it to this console's port; permit TCP from it to port 22 (SSH); permit established TCP; permit UDP replies; permit ICMP.
- On the right, the entries as they will be created, ending with what happens to anything else. Warnings for an empty extended list (once applied it drops everything, this console included) and for a copied extended list that doesn't permit this console's port.
- "Create list" or "Create list with N entries". The new list is under Lists not in use until you apply it. If an entry fails, the list is still created and the page says which entries are missing.

### Examples

- Allow SSH only from the office network `192.168.1.0/24`, and the console, on eth0:
  1. Under Lists not in use, click "New List", choose "Allow services", keep "Basic protection (recommended)", enter the Management network `192.168.1.0/24`, and click "Create list with 5 entries".
  2. On that list, click "Apply to an interface", enter `eth0`, choose the new list in Stage 2, and click "Apply".
  3. On the eth0 tab, open "Test a packet", click SSH, and enter a source outside `192.168.1.0/24` and a destination address of the device: it should say Dropped, by the implicit deny. A source inside it should say Passed.
  4. Click "Save Config".
- Block one malicious host on eth0: on the eth0 tab, in Stage 1 click "Add Entry" (or "Add a standard list" first if there is none), keep Deny (block) and Host, enter `203.0.113.66`, and click "Add Entry". Then "Save Config". Other traffic is unaffected, since a standard list only drops what it denies.

## Saving the configuration

- Access list changes take effect at once but live only in the device's running state. The "Unsaved changes" tag in the header means the running configuration differs from the one the device loads when it starts.
- "Save Config" saves the running configuration, so the device loads it at its next start, and the "Unsaved changes" tag goes away.
- If you undo a change by hand, the tag goes away too, since the configuration matches the saved one again.
- Only administrators can save the configuration.
- If a change cuts off your access to the console (for example an extended list that doesn't permit it), restart the device: it starts with the saved configuration, without the unsaved change. This works only if the change wasn't saved with "Save Config".

## Common questions

- I added an entry but the traffic isn't blocked. Open the interface's tab: its status must say "Enforced", and the list must be shown in a stage there (a list under Lists not in use does nothing). Use "Test a packet" with the traffic's addresses and ports to see which entry decides; look for "Never matches" notes; check the interface name isn't "Not on this device".
- All my traffic is blocked after I applied an extended list. In an extended list, traffic that matches no entry is dropped, so end the list with a permit entry for the rest, such as `permit ip any any`. A standard list doesn't do this: it only drops what it denies.
- I can't see the access lists. Your account is a user, not an administrator; only administrators can view or change them.
- My rules were gone after the device restarted. The changes weren't saved with "Save Config". Ask an administrator to save after making changes.
- I can't see the "Save Config" button. Your account is a user, not an administrator; ask an administrator to save.
- "Network error. Please try again later." The browser can't reach the device. Check your network connection and reload the page.
- "Request failed" or another error after an action. Try again later; if it keeps happening, contact the administrator.
